theme: The LORD has made known his salvation
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 98. It is a joyful song about God’s victory and salvation, revealed to the nations. Isaac Watts’s hymn “Joy to the World” is based on this psalm.
settingTheScene: Psalm 98 is a psalm without a title, but it builds on Psalm 96 and 97 and continues the theme of the LORD’s kingship. It is filled with music: new songs, harps, trumpets, and the sea clapping. It is read at Christmas by many churches. In the context of Acts, it stresses that God has made his salvation known “in the sight of the nations.”
observation: “Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things!” (v. 1).
“His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him” (v. 1).
“The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations” (v. 2).
“He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel” (v. 3).
“All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (v. 3).
“Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises!” (v. 4).
“Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together” (v. 8).
“Before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with the same call as Psalm 96, a new song, but gives a different reason: “for he has done marvelous things.” Chief among these is salvation. “His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.” The arm of the LORD is a picture of his strength to deliver, as in the exodus. Notice the phrase “for him”: God’s victory is not borrowed from anyone. He won it himself.

Verse 2 gives the missionary side: “The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations.” God’s salvation is public. It is not hidden in a corner. And verse 3 shows how the two sides fit together: God remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. And as a result, all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. His covenant faithfulness to Israel is the way he brings salvation to the world. This is the story of Acts: the promises made to Israel are fulfilled in Jesus, and through him, the nations see the salvation of God. Simeon sang this when he held the child in the temple: “My eyes have seen your salvation… a light for revelation to the Gentiles.”

Verses 4 to 6 call all the earth to make a joyful noise with lyre, trumpets, and the horn, before the King. And verses 7 to 9 extend the chorus to creation: the sea roars, the rivers clap their hands, and the hills sing for joy together, because the LORD is coming to judge the earth. Creation itself longs for the coming of the King (Romans 8:19-22). When he comes, creation will be set right.

Reading this psalm with Acts reminds us that the church’s mission is accompanied by joy. We are not announcing a threat. We are announcing a victory. The right hand and the holy arm have worked salvation in the cross and the empty tomb, and the whole world is invited to see it and sing.
connection: Exodus 15:1-18 is the original victory song. Isaiah 52:10 says all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. Isaiah 59:16 and 63:5 speak of his arm bringing salvation. Luke 2:30-32 is Simeon’s song. Luke 1:68-75 is Zechariah’s song. Romans 8:19-23 describes creation groaning and longing. Revelation 15:3-4 is the song of Moses and the Lamb. Isaac Watts’s “Joy to the World” paraphrases this psalm.
application:
Sing “Joy to the World” aloud, even out of season.

Tell someone about a marvelous thing the LORD has done. Be specific.

Look at creation today, a tree or a hill or the sky, and imagine it singing to its Lord.
prayerPrompts: Sing to the LORD a new song for the marvelous things he has done.
Thank him for making his salvation known.
Ask him to help you break forth in joyous song.
